title: Controllers in ASP.NET Core
description: Understand what controllers are, how to create them, and how they use routing to connect URLs to action methods.

data.text: What Is a Controller?

A controller is a C# class that inherits from ControllerBase. It receives HTTP requests, processes them, and returns responses. The class must be named with the Controller suffix and placed in the `Controllers` folder.

terms.definition: A C# class that inherits from ControllerBase. It groups related action methods and sits between the browser and your data.
The base class for controllers without view support. Provides properties like `HttpContext`, `User`, and ModelState.
A class that inherits from ControllerBase and adds view-related features like `View()`, ViewBag, and `TempData`.
The system that maps incoming URLs to specific controller action methods.

data.text: Creating a Controller
Create a new C# class inside the `Controllers` folder that inherits from Controller. Add public methods — those are your action methods. Each action method should return IActionResult.

data.title: A minimal controller
data.content: A controller with a single action that returns a view.

data.text: Controller Naming and the [controller] Token

The name of the controller class determines the `[controller]` route token. For example, HomeController maps to `home`, and `ProductsController` maps to `products`. The convention strips the Controller suffix and lowercases the remainder.

data.title: Rule of Thumb
data.text: Name controllers after the resource they manage: HomeController for the home page, `ProductsController` for products, AccountController for authentication. Place them in the `Controllers` folder.
Action Methods

Action methods are public methods inside a controller. They are the entry points for user requests. By default, any public method is treated as an action method. The method name becomes the action name in the URL.
Controller Return Types
The simplest return type is IActionResult. For now, focus on two common values: `View()` and `RedirectToAction()`. You will see more in later modules.
Controller with Multiple Actions
A controller can have as many action methods as needed. Each method handles a different URL or user intent:

data.title: A controller with multiple actions
data.content: HomeController with Index and About actions.

data.text: Mapping URLs to Controllers
By default, ASP.NET Core uses convention-based routing to map URLs. A URL like `/Home/Index` maps to the `Index` action on HomeController. The URL structure is `/ControllerName/ActionName`.
If you want more control over the URL structure, you can use attribute routing. Instead of relying on the default convention, you decorate controllers and actions with `[Route]` attributes.

data.title: Attribute routing on a controller
data.content: Use [Route] to define custom URL patterns for a controller.

data.text: With the `[Route("[controller]/[action]")]` attribute, the `ProductsController.Index()` action responds to `/Products/Index`, and `ProductsController.Details(5)` responds to `/Products/Details/5`.
Controller Anatomy

rows: Groups related actions and holds shared logic.
Handle individual requests and return responses.
Define custom URL patterns for controllers and actions.
Provides core properties like `HttpContext`, `User`, and ModelState.
Adds view support with `View()`, ViewBag, and `TempData`.

data.text: MVC and Web API Controllers
ASP.NET Core supports two main controller types: MVC controllers (for HTML views) and API controllers (for JSON endpoints). You can mix both in the same project.

data.title: API controller
data.content: An ApiController that returns JSON data.

data.text: The Controller Class
The Controller class inherits from ControllerBase and adds view support with `View()`, ViewBag, and `TempData`. It is the base class for MVC controllers.
The [controller] Token
The `[controller]` token is automatically replaced by the controller's class name without the Controller suffix. For HomeController, `[controller]` becomes `home`.
The [action] Token
The `[action]` token is automatically replaced by the action method's name. For the `About` method, `[action]` becomes `about`.
Route Precedence
When multiple routes match a URL, ASP.NET Core selects the most specific one. Action-level routes take precedence over controller-level routes.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Controllers are C# classes that inherit from ControllerBase or Controller.
Action methods are public methods that handle HTTP requests and return responses.
The `Controllers` folder is the conventional location for controller classes.
The `[controller]` token maps to the controller's class name minus the Controller suffix.
Use `[Route]` attributes to define custom URL patterns for controllers and actions.
MVC controllers inherit from Controller and support views; API controllers inherit from ControllerBase and return JSON.
data.takeaway: Controllers are the entry point for every HTTP request. Mastering them is the first step toward building complete web applications.
